claim: A hallmark of electrophysiological brain activity is its 1/f-like spectrum where power decreases with increasing frequency.
source: A hallmark of electrophysiological brain activity is its 1/f-like spectrum – power decreases with increasing frequency.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about electrophysiological brain activity and is supported by citations in the subsequent text.

claim: The spectral exponent in invasively recorded neural populations reflects the balance of excitatory to inhibitory neural activity (E:I balance).
source: The steepness of this 'roll-off' is approximated by the spectral exponent, which in invasively recorded neural populations reflects the balance of excitatory to inhibitory neural activity (E:I balance).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on invasive recordings, as referenced throughout the manuscript.

claim: The EEG spectral exponent of non-invasive electroencephalography recordings is highly sensitive to general anaesthesia-driven changes in E:I balance.
source: Here, we first establish that the spectral exponent of non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) recordings is highly sensitive to general (i.e., anaesthesia-driven) changes in E:I balance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the anaesthesia dataset analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: EEG spectral exponents are sensitive to the focus of selective attention during an audio-visual detection task.
source: Building on the EEG spectral exponent as a viable marker of E:I, we then demonstrate its sensitivity to the focus of selective attention in an EEG experiment during which participants detected targets in simultaneous audio-visual noise.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the multisensory detection task described in the manuscript.

claim: EEG spectral exponents over auditory and visual sensory cortices tracked auditory and visual stimulus spectral exponents, respectively.
source: In addition to these endogenous changes in E:I balance, EEG spectral exponents over auditory and visual sensory cortices also tracked auditory and visual stimulus spectral exponents, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the relationship between stimulus and EEG spectral exponents.

claim: Individuals' degree of selective stimulus–brain coupling in spectral exponents predicted behavioural performance.
source: Individuals' degree of this selective stimulus–brain coupling in spectral exponents predicted behavioural performance.
evidence: This is supported by the partial least squares analysis correlating neural tracking with behavioral performance.

claim: Non-invasive recordings of electrical brain activity represent the aggregated post-synaptic activity of large cortical neuronal ensembles.
source: Non-invasive recordings of electrical brain activity represent the aggregated post-synaptic activity of large cortical neuronal ensembles (Buzsáki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Buzsáki et al., 2012.

claim: Frequency spectra of electrophysiological recordings commonly display quasi-linearly decreasing power with increasing frequency in log/log space.
source: Frequency spectra of electrophysiological recordings commonly display quasi-linearly decreasing power with increasing frequency (in log/log space; see Figure 1; see Miller et al., 2009; Voytek et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2009 and Voytek et al., 2015, and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: In humans, the decrease in power with frequency is superimposed by several peaks, of which the most prominent is typically in the range of alpha oscillations (~8–12 Hz).
source: In humans, this decrease is super positioned by several peaks, of which the most prominent is typically in the range of alpha oscillations (~8–12 Hz; see Buzsáki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Buzsáki et al., 2013 and is established knowledge about human EEG.

claim: The overall decrease in power as a function of frequency reflects aperiodic as opposed to oscillatory activity.
source: The overall decrease in power as a function of frequency, f, reflects aperiodic as opposed to oscillatory activity; the steepness of such 1/fχ spectra can be captured by the spectral exponent χ, wherein smaller values reflect flatter spectra.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the nature of the spectral exponent and is supported by the methodological framework used in the study.

claim: Inter-individual differences in the steepness of human EEG power spectral densities, estimated by the spectral exponent χ, are related to chronological age, behavioural performance, and display stable inter-individual differences.
source: Importantly, inter-individual differences in the steepness of human electroencephalography (EEG), power spectral densities (PSD), estimated by the spectral exponent χ, are related to chronological age, behavioural performance, and display stable inter-individual differences (Dave et al., 2018; Donoghue et al., 2020; Sheehan et al., 2018; Voytek et al., 2015; Waschke et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Intra-individual variations in EEG spectral exponents have been reported as a function of overall arousal level and activation.
source: Intra-individual variations in EEG spectral exponents have been reported as a function of overall arousal level and activation (Colombo et al., 2019; Lendner et al., 2020; Podvalny et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Colombo et al., 2019; Lendner et al., 2020; and Podvalny et al., 2015.

claim: Based on computational models and invasive recordings of neural activity, electrophysiological spectral exponents capture the balance of excitatory and inhibitory neural activity (E:I).
source: Based on computational models and invasive recordings of neural activity, it has been demonstrated that electrophysiological spectral exponents capture the balance of excitatory and inhibitory neural activity (E:I; Gao et al., 2017), with recent causal, optogenetic work showing that lower exponents are mechanistically linked to increased E:I balance (Chini et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gao et al., 2017 and Chini et al., 2021.

claim: Lower spectral exponents are mechanistically linked to increased E:I balance.
source: Based on computational models and invasive recordings of neural activity, it has been demonstrated that electrophysiological spectral exponents capture the balance of excitatory and inhibitory neural activity (E:I; Gao et al., 2017), with recent causal, optogenetic work showing that lower exponents are mechanistically linked to increased E:I balance (Chini et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chini et al., 2021, which used optogenetic methods.

claim: An attentional shift towards a given sensory modality is suggested to entail desynchronized activity in cortical areas that process information from the currently attended domain.
source: An attentional shift towards a given sensory modality is suggested to entail desynchronized activity (i.e., reduced low-frequency oscillations and increased high-frequency power) in cortical areas that process information from the currently attended domain (Cohen and Maunsell, 2011; Harris and Thiele, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cohen and Maunsell, 2011 and Harris and Thiele, 2011.

claim: Shifts in desynchronization likely trace back to an attention-related change in E:I balance towards excitation.
source: These shifts in desynchronization likely trace back to an attention-related change in E:I balance towards excitation (Harris and Thiele, 2011; Zagha and McCormick, 2014), which is thought to manifest in a reduction of spectral exponents (Gao et al., 2017; Waschke et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harris and Thiele, 2011; Zagha and McCormick, 2014; Gao et al., 2017; and Waschke et al., 2019.

claim: Selective attention should result in a topographically specific decrease of spectral exponents if EEG spectral exponents represent a sensitive approximation of E:I balance.
source: If EEG spectral exponents indeed represent a sensitive approximation of E:I balance, selective attention should also result in a topographically specific decrease of exponents.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from prior knowledge about E:I balance and attention.

claim: Propofol anaesthesia led to an overall increase in EEG power which was especially pronounced in the alpha-beta range.
source: Here, propofol anaesthesia led to an overall increase in EEG power which was especially pronounced in the alpha-beta range.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Ketamine anaesthesia decreased the frequency of alpha oscillations and suppressed power in the beta range.
source: Ketamine anaesthesia decreased the frequency of alpha oscillations and supressed power in the beta range.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: EEG spectral exponents increased under propofol anaesthesia in all participants.
source: Importantly, however, EEG spectral exponents that were estimated while accounting for changes in oscillatory activity increased under propofol and decreased under ketamine anaesthesia in all participants (both ppermuted < 0.0009, Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 1.

claim: EEG spectral exponents decreased under ketamine anaesthesia in all participants.
source: Importantly, however, EEG spectral exponents that were estimated while accounting for changes in oscillatory activity increased under propofol and decreased under ketamine anaesthesia in all participants (both ppermuted < 0.0009, Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Participants performed better during visual compared to auditory trials in the multisensory detection task.
source: While training and adaptive adjustments of difficulty (see methods for details) ensured that the task was challenging but doable in both modalities (average accuracy ≥ 70 %), participants performed better during visual compared to auditory trials (t23 = 5.8, p = 7 × 10–6, Cohen's d = 1.18; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: EEG spectral exponents at occipital electrodes strongly decreased under visual compared to auditory attention.
source: Notably, EEG spectral exponents at occipital electrodes strongly decreased (spectra flattened) under visual compared to auditory attention (t23 = 7.4, p = 1 × 10–7, Cohen's d = 1.52; see Figure 3B), while this was the case to a much lesser extent at central electrodes (t23 = 2.6, p = 0.01, Cohen's d = 0.54).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A main effect of auditory stimulus exponent was found at a set of four central electrodes.
source: A main effect of auditory stimulus exponent, capturing the trial-wise positive linear relationship between auditory AM spectral exponents and EEG spectral exponents (i.e., neural tracking) was found at a set of four central electrodes (all z > 3.5, all pcorrected< 0.02; see Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A positive main effect of visual stimulus exponent was present at a set of three occipital electrodes.
source: Similarly, a positive main effect of visual stimulus exponent was present at a set of three occipital electrodes (all z > 3.7, all pcorrected< 0.01; see Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: EEG spectral exponents displayed a topographically resolved tracking of stimulus exponents of both modalities.
source: Hence, EEG spectral exponents displayed a topographically resolved tracking of stimulus exponents of both modalities.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing modality-specific tracking at different electrode locations.

claim: Auditory stimulus tracking increased significantly when participants focused their attention on auditory stimuli.
source: Paired t-tests comparing standardized regression coefficients that represent the strength of neural stimulus tracking revealed a significant increase of auditory stimulus tracking under auditory attention (t23 = 2.4, p = 0.03, Cohen's d = 0.49).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the interaction between attention and stimulus tracking.

claim: Visual stimulus tracking did not significantly improve under visual attention, though the direction of the effect was the same.
source: Visual stimulus tracking did not significantly improve under visual attention, though the direction of the effect was the same (t23 = 1.0, p =0 .33, Cohen's d = 0.20).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis showing a non-significant trend.

claim: Conventional estimates of sensory evoked EEG activity were insensitive to the AM spectral exponents of presented stimuli.
source: In contrast to 1/f EEG exponents, conventional metrics of sensory evoked EEG activity were thus insensitive to the AM spectral exponents of presented stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of ERPs which showed no significant tracking of stimulus exponents.

claim: At the overall latent level, both auditory and visual stimulus tracking were significantly correlated with performance across subjects.
source: At the overall latent level, both auditory (rho = 0.49, p = 0.016) and visual stimulus tracking (rho = 0.43, p = 0.035) were significantly correlated with performance across subjects (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the partial least squares analysis and data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Auditory stimulus tracking was positively correlated with auditory response speed.
source: In detail, auditory stimulus tracking was positively correlated with auditory response speed (rho = 0.30, CI = [0.03, 0.64]) but negatively correlated with visual accuracy (rho = –0.28, CI = [–0.62, –0.06]) and response speed (rho = –0.36, CI = [–0.73, –0.17]).
evidence: This is supported by the partial least squares analysis showing specific correlations.

claim: Visual stimulus tracking was positively linked with visual accuracy and response speed.
source: Analogously, visual stimulus tracking was positively linked with visual accuracy (rho = 0.31, CI = [0.15, 0.68]) and response speed (rho = 0.35, CI = [0.11, 0.72]; see Figure 5A), but showed no significant relationship with auditory performance.
evidence: This is supported by the partial least squares analysis and data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Participants who displayed stronger neural tracking of AM stimulus spectra also performed better.
source: Taken together, participants who displayed stronger neural tracking of AM stimulus spectra also performed better.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the correlation analyses between tracking and performance.

claim: The behavioural benefit of stimulus tracking was modality-specific.
source: However, the behavioural benefit of stimulus tracking was modality-specific: performance in one sensory domain (e.g., auditory) only benefited from tracking within that domain, but not in the other (e.g., visual).
evidence: This is an inference from the pattern of correlations showing domain-specific benefits.

claim: Visual detection performance was slower and less accurate in individuals who displayed strong neural tracking of 1/f-like auditory stimulus features.
source: Instead, visual detection performance was slower and less accurate in individuals who displayed strong neural tracking of 1/f-like auditory stimulus features.
evidence: This is supported by the negative correlations between auditory tracking and visual performance.

claim: Early ERP components at electrode Oz were increased during visual attention.
source: While there was no significant attention-related ERP difference found at electrode Cz, early ERP components at electrode Oz were increased during visual attention (~.08 –.15 s post-stimulus, pcorrected < 0.05; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Alpha power increased from visual to auditory attention in a region-specific manner, with stronger increases over occipital cortical areas.
source: Hence, alpha power increased from visual to auditory attention in a region-specific manner, with stronger increases over occipital cortical areas (see spectra in Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by ANOVA results and data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Propofol is known to commonly result in a net increase of inhibition.
source: Importantly, however, propofol is known to commonly result in a net increase of inhibition (Concas et al., 1991; Franks, 2008) whereas ketamine results in a relative increase of excitation (Deane et al., 2020; Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Concas et al., 1991 and Franks, 2008.

claim: Ketamine results in a relative increase of excitation.
source: Importantly, however, propofol is known to commonly result in a net increase of inhibition (Concas et al., 1991; Franks, 2008) whereas ketamine results in a relative increase of excitation (Deane et al., 2020; Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deane et al., 2020 and Miller et al., 2016.

claim: Propofol anaesthesia should lead to an increase in the spectral exponent (steepening of the spectrum) based on invasive work and single cell modelling.
source: In accordance with invasive work and single cell modelling (Chini et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2017), propofol anaesthesia should thus lead to an increase in the spectral exponent (steepening of the spectrum) and ketamine anaesthesia to a decrease (flattening).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on citations to Chini et al., 2021 and Gao et al., 2017.

claim: Ketamine anaesthesia should lead to a decrease in the spectral exponent (flattening) based on invasive work and single cell modelling.
source: In accordance with invasive work and single cell modelling (Chini et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2017), propofol anaesthesia should thus lead to an increase in the spectral exponent (steepening of the spectrum) and ketamine anaesthesia to a decrease (flattening).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on citations to Chini et al., 2021 and Gao et al., 2017.

claim: The effect of anaesthesia on EEG spectral exponents is expected to be highly consistent and display little topographical variation.
source: Based on previous results, the effect of anaesthesia on EEG spectral exponents is expected to be highly consistent and display little topographical variation (Lendner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on citation to Lendner et al., 2020.

claim: Speech signals show a pronounced 1/f shape within their amplitude modulation spectrum.
source: Indeed, even speech signals show a pronounced 1/f shape within their amplitude modulation (AM) spectrum (see e.g., Attias and Schreiner, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Attias and Schreiner, 1997.

claim: There is first non-human in vitro and in vivo evidence for neural tracking of 1/f sensory signals.
source: However, despite first non-human in vitro and in vivo evidence for such a neural tracking of 1/f sensory signals (Nozaki et al., 1999; Qu et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2005), it is unclear at present if the 1/f structure of sensory inputs is tracked by 1/f-like non-invasively recorded neural activity in humans.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nozaki et al., 1999; Qu et al., 2019; and Yu et al., 2005.

claim: Postsynaptic potentials in sensory cortical areas could temporally align and scale with the magnitude of sensory stimuli and hence result in a mimicking of the stimulus spectrum.
source: Postsynaptic potentials in sensory cortical areas could temporally align and scale with the magnitude of sensory stimuli and hence result in a mimicking of the stimulus spectrum, as has been suggested for oscillatory signals and steady state evoked potentials (e.g., Norcia et al., 2015) and broadband signals or speech (Lalor et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by citations to Norcia et al., 2015 and Lalor et al., 2009.

claim: The spectral exponent of the human brain will capture and prove not only endogenous changes in E:I balance but also reflect statistical features of the sensory input.
source: It thus appears plausible that the spectral exponent of the human brain will capture and prove not only endogenous changes in E:I balance but also reflect statistical features of the sensory input.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from the mechanisms discussed.

claim: Propofol-induced increases of spectral exponents likely trace back to strengthened inhibition via increased activity at gamma-Aminobutyric acid receptors and hence a reduced E:I balance as compared to quiet wakefulness.
source: Increased spectral exponents under propofol likely trace back to strengthened inhibition via increased activity at gamma-Aminobutyric acid receptors (GABAergic activity) and hence a reduced E:I balance as compared to quiet wakefulness (Concas et al., 1991; Franks, 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on citations to Concas et al., 1991 and Franks, 2008.

claim: Ketamine-induced decreases of spectral exponents likely depict the outcome of overall decreased inhibition that is caused by the blocking of excitatory N-methyl-d-aspartate receptors and an associated decrease in GABA release, resulting in an increased E:I balance.
source: Furthermore, ketamine-induced decreases of spectral exponents likely depict the outcome of overall decreased inhibition that is caused by the blocking of excitatory N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptors and an associated decrease in GABA release, resulting in an increased E:I balance (Behrens et al., 2007; Deane et al., 2020; Franks, 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on citations to Behrens et al., 2007; Deane et al., 2020; and Franks, 2008.

claim: The EEG spectral exponent as a remote, summary measure of brain electric activity cannot quantify local E:I in a given neural population.
source: While the EEG spectral exponent as a remote, summary measure of brain electric activity can obviously not quantify local E:I in a given neural population, the non-invasive approximation demonstrated here enables inferences on global neural processes previously only accessible in animals and using invasive methods.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on the nature of EEG measurements.

claim: The non-invasive approximation of E:I demonstrated here enables inferences on global neural processes previously only accessible in animals and using invasive methods.
source: While the EEG spectral exponent as a remote, summary measure of brain electric activity can obviously not quantify local E:I in a given neural population, the non-invasive approximation demonstrated here enables inferences on global neural processes previously only accessible in animals and using invasive methods.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: The absence of a comparable effect for auditory attention at central electrodes potentially traces back to the varying sensitivity of EEG recordings to different cortical sources.
source: The absence of a comparable effect for auditory attention at central electrodes potentially traces back to the varying sensitivity of EEG recordings to different cortical sources.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the observed pattern of results.

claim: Central electrodes capture auditory cortical activity but are positioned far away from their dominant source.
source: Central electrodes capture auditory cortical activity but are positioned far away from their dominant source ( Huotilainen et al., 1998; Stropahl et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huotilainen et al., 1998 and Stropahl et al., 2018.

claim: Occipital electrodes are sensitive to visual cortex activity and are directly positioned above it.
source: Occipital electrodes, however, are sensitive to visual cortex activity and are directly positioned above it (Hagler et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hagler et al., 2009.

claim: The employed spectral parameterization approach enabled separation of 1/f like signals from oscillatory activity and hence offered distinct estimates of spectral exponent and alpha power that would otherwise have been conflated.
source: The employed spectral parameterization approach enabled to us to separate 1/f like signals from oscillatory activity and hence offered distinct estimates of spectral exponent and alpha power that would otherwise have been conflated (Donoghue et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citation to Donoghue et al., 2020.

claim: Bursts of thalamic activity that project towards sensory cortical areas might sculpt cortical excitability in an attention-dependent manner by inhibiting irrelevant distracting information.
source: On the one hand, bursts of thalamic activity that project towards sensory cortical areas might sculpt cortical excitability in an attention-dependent manner by inhibiting irrelevant distracting information (Klimesch et al., 2007; Saalmann and Kastner, 2011).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by citations to Klimesch et al., 2007 and Saalmann and Kastner, 2011.

claim: Tonic thalamic activity likely drives cortical desynchronization via glutamatergic projections and, with attentional focus, results in boosted representations of stimulus information within brain signals.
source: On the other hand, tonic thalamic activity likely drives cortical desynchronization via glutamatergic projections and, with attentional focus, results in boosted representations of stimulus information within brain signals (Cohen and Maunsell, 2011; Harris and Thiele, 2011; Sherman, 2001).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by citations to Cohen and Maunsell, 2011; Harris and Thiele, 2011; and Sherman, 2001.

claim: The tracking of stimulus spectral exponents displayed distinct central and occipital topographies for auditory and visual stimuli, respectively.
source: The neural tracking of stimulus spectra displayed distinct central and occipital topographies for auditory and visual stimuli, respectively (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The spatial distinctiveness of both tracking patterns strongly suggests separate cortical origins.
source: Of course, current source density transforms of sensor-level EEG topographies as used here do not represent definitive evidence for specific cortical sources. Yet, the spatial distinctiveness of both tracking patterns strongly suggests separate cortical origins.
evidence: This is an inference from the topographical patterns observed.

claim: The topographies of stimulus tracking strongly resemble those of sensory processing in auditory and visual sensory cortical areas, respectively.
source: Furthermore, the topographies of stimulus tracking strongly resemble those of sensory processing in auditory and visual sensory cortical areas, respectively (Iemi et al., 2019; Waschke et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Iemi et al., 2019 and Waschke et al., 2019.

claim: The representation of stimulus spectra in the EEG does not trace back to an alignment of true oscillatory neural activity and oscillatory stimulus features (entrainment in the narrow sense).
source: First, it is important to emphasise that the representation of stimulus spectra in the EEG does not trace back to an alignment of true oscillatory neural activity and oscillatory stimulus features, commonly referred to as 'entrainment' in the narrow sense (Obleser and Kayser, 2019) entrainment in the narrow sense would be contingent on the presence of true endogenous oscillatory activity within recorded EEG that progressively synchronizes its phase to the phase of exogenous stimulus oscillations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of the stimuli used (stochastic, not sinusoidal).

claim: Presented stimuli were stochastic in nature and without clear sinusoidal signals, preventing narrow-sense oscillatory entrainment from taking place.
source: Here, presented stimuli were stochastic in nature and without clear sinusoidal signals, preventing narrow-sense oscillatory entrainment from taking place.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Neural tracking of the statistical properties of random noise time-series might emerge via the temporal alignment of high amplitude stimulus periods with high amplitude neural activity periods.
source: Neural tracking of the statistical properties of random noise time-series might emerge via the temporal alignment of high amplitude stimulus periods with high amplitude neural activity periods, a mechanism similar to the one implied in the generation of steady-state evoked potentials (SSEPs; Norcia et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by citation to Norcia et al., 2015.

claim: Phase and amplitude time-courses of stimuli were dissimilar across trials, preventing phase-locked evoked activity.
source: First, phase and amplitude time-courses of stimuli were dissimilar across trials, preventing phase-locked evoked activity, a hallmark of SSEP generation (Vialatte et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and its implications.

claim: The observed neural tracking of AM spectral exponents does not emerge via a neural adaptation to constant amplitude spectra or trial-wise differences in evoked responses.
source: Hence, the observed neural tracking of AM spectral exponents does not emerge via a neural adaptation to constant amplitude spectra or trial-wise differences in evoked responses.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental design and analysis approach.

claim: Auditory TRFs were unreliable.
source: However, auditory TRFs were unreliable (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Visual TRFs enabled significant stimulus reconstruction.
source: Visual TRFs on the other hand enabled significant stimulus reconstruction and were used within a simplified proof-of-concept model to predict EEG signals that indeed mimicked the spectral properties of stimuli (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The non-predictiveness of auditory TRFs potentially traces back to an insufficient signal-to-noise ratio and limited training data.
source: The non-predictiveness of auditory TRFs potentially traces back to an insufficient signal-to-noise ratio and limited training data.
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for the observed results.

claim: EEG spectral exponents might capture the consequences of non-linear interactions between stimulus input and neural response by focusing on their spectral representation across a wide frequency range.
source: In general, EEG spectral exponents might also capture the consequences of non-linear interactions between stimulus input and neural response by focusing on their spectral representation across a wide frequency range.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanisms underlying the observed effects.

claim: Time- and spectrally based approaches of stimulus tracking might capture similar aspects of postsynaptic neural activity that align with sensory input during early processing.
source: Hence, time- and spectrally based approaches of stimulus tracking might indeed capture similar aspects of postsynaptic neural activity that align with sensory input during early processing.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of different analysis approaches.

claim: The topography of the between-subject neuro-behavioural correlations does not display peaks at the central or occipital regions that were found to show significant stimulus tracking.
source: Of note, the topography of the between-subject neuro-behavioural correlations does not display peaks at the central or occipital regions that were found to show significant stimulus tracking.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The fronto-central topography of the between subject correlation is suggestive of sources in frontal cortex, which have been shown to track multi-sensory information.
source: Indeed, the fronto-central topography of the between subject correlation is suggestive of sources in frontal cortex, which have been shown to track multi-sensory information (Ghazanfar and Schroeder, 2006; Senkowski et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Ghazanfar and Schroeder, 2006 and Senkowski et al., 2007.

claim: Prefrontal cortex activity has been found to represent information about the frequency content of auditory, visual, and somatosensory stimuli.
source: Furthermore, prefrontal cortex activity that gives rise to highly similar frontal topographies (Figure 5) has been found to represent information about the frequency content of auditory, visual, and somatosensory stimuli (Spitzer and Blankenburg, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Spitzer and Blankenburg, 2012.

claim: The positive link between neural stimulus tracking and performance at fronto-central electrodes points to the behavioural relevance of higher-level stimulus features represented in a supramodal fashion.
source: Thus, the positive link between neural stimulus tracking and performance at fronto-central electrodes points to the behavioural relevance of higher-level stimulus features represented in a supramodal fashion.
evidence: This is an inference from the pattern of results.

claim: Single trial parameterization provided good fits in all subjects and at all electrodes.
source: Note that single trial parameterization provided good fits in all subjects and at all electrodes.
evidence: This is a methodological observation about the quality of the spectral fitting.

claim: Mean R-squared values exceeded 0.84 at all electrodes for single trial parameterizations of power spectra.
source: Single trial parameterizations of power spectra provided excellent fits for the vast majority of trials (mean R2> 0.84 at all electrodes, see Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.
